title: ADAS Regulations overview: What every automaker needs to know
summary: Here is a quick look at the most important regulatory developments shaping ADAS deployment in 2026 and beyond.
body_text: Advanced driver assistance systems continue to evolve, with ADAS regulations in 2026 becoming a defining force in how new vehicle platforms are designed and deployed. What was once a mix of voluntary guidelines is now taking shape as structured, enforceable policy across major markets. Here is a quick look at the most important regulatory developments shaping ADAS deployment in 2026 and beyond. The second wave of GSR takes effect in Europe Europe remains one of the most structured regulatory environments for vehicle safety technology. The General Safety Regulation (GSR) introduced a broad set of mandatory safety systems across new vehicles sold in the European Union. The initial phase applied primarily to new vehicle types, with requirements extended in July 2024 to cover all new vehicles sold in the EU, including existing models. Additional requirements are expected to take effect in July 2026.These requirements include technologies such as autonomous emergency braking (AEB), intelligent speed assistance (ISA), driver drowsiness and attention monitoring and Advanced Driver Distraction Warning. For automakers, this means that driver assistance capabilities are no longer optional features. They are becoming baseline safety infrastructure across the European vehicle market. Because many global platforms are developed with European homologation in mind, these regulations often influence vehicle architecture well beyond the EU. Platforms that consolidate these functions, rather than treating each mandate as a separate integration problem, are increasingly becoming central to how OEMs think about compliance at scale. To align with automakers' growing regulatory pressures, Mobileye’s Surround ADAS , its flagship comprehensive ADAS solution, alleviates some of these pressures through a consolidated architecture that includes 360° coverage and the latest regulatory requirements met in one solution. The rise of driver control assistance systems Driver Control Assistance Systems (DCAS) have become increasingly common across today's vehicles. They are defined as systems that assist with both steering and speed control on a sustained basis, without taking over the full driving task. It is the evolving capability of DCAS, however, that is leading regulators to focus more closely on how drivers engage with these systems, ensuring that drivers remain attentive and ready to intervene at all times. As a result, features and technologies that support this are becoming a standard part of today's driver assistance systems. Examples include, Driver Monitoring Systems (DMS), safe system fallback strategies, clear human machine interface communication. At Mobileye, we believe the most effective approach to driver monitoring goes beyond compliance. It starts with thoughtful system design. The Mobileye DMS™ is not a standalone add-on, but rather fused with ADAS, designed to work in concert with the vehicle’s external sensing system, created to enhance responsiveness and situational awareness. Guidance over mandates in the United States In contrast to Europe's more prescriptive approach, the United States continues to rely largely on safety standards and voluntary frameworks rather than broad mandates. Federal regulators emphasize safety reporting, transparency around automated systems, and voluntary commitments, while individual states retain authority over key aspects of automated vehicle deployment. This creates a more flexible but fragmented regulatory environment, where automakers must navigate a mix of federal guidance and state level policies. As automated capabilities continue to evolve, further clarification around driver assistance classifications, supervision requirements, and safety evaluation is likely to emerge. China: accelerating intelligent driving regulation China is rapidly developing its regulatory framework for highly automated and autonomous driving systems, with China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) presenting a draft of new safety requirements set to be implemented by July 2027. The draft targets vehicles operating at SAE Level 3 and Level 4 automation, and will replace previous voluntary guidelines with mandatory safety requirements. Regulatory documents increasingly reference the classification term "Combined Driver Assistance Systems" (CDAS) as part of China's structured approach to defining automation levels. The country has also established pilot programs for automated driving in urban environments, allowing regulators to iterate quickly while supporting rapid technology adoption. Given the size and strategic importance of the Chinese automotive market, these developments are expected to play a significant role in shaping global autonomous driving technology roadmaps. A global shift toward accountable automation Despite regional differences, several clear trends are emerging across regulatory frameworks. First, driver assistance systems are moving from optional features toward mandatory baseline safety capabilities. Second, regulators are placing greater emphasis on driver supervision and system accountability, particularly as vehicles approach higher levels of automation. Finally, regulatory frameworks are increasingly focused on establishing structured pathways toward automated driving, rather than allowing technology to evolve without clear definitions. For automakers, these trends reinforce the need for vehicle platforms that can scale across markets while meeting increasingly complex safety expectations. *Provided for general informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice or an interpretation of any applicable laws or regulations

title: How Is India’s EV Charging Infrastructure Evolving for EV Adoption?
summary: Explore EV charging infrastructure in India, including EV charging stations, AC and DC chargers, charging software, hardware, and franchise opportunities.
body_text: You may be surprised by how quickly EV charging infrastructure in India has evolved. Just a few years ago, public charging stations were limited, long-distance travel required careful planning, and home charging options were still developing. Today, the landscape looks very different. The shift is being driven by rising EV adoption. According to Vahan Dashboard data (July 2026), passenger EV penetration increased from 4.8% in June 2025 to 7.7% in June 2026, while monthly electric car sales reached 31,388 units in June 2026. These trends reflect the continued growth of India’s passenger EV market and the increasing need for accessible, reliable EV charging infrastructure across the country. Government initiatives, private investment, and advances in charging technology have accelerated the expansion of EV charging stations across cities, highways, residential communities, workplaces, and commercial spaces. As more electric vehicles enter Indian roads, the focus is shifting from simply installing more chargers to building a connected charging ecosystem that is reliable, accessible, and scalable enough to support future demand. EV charging infrastructure is therefore about much more than installing chargers. It includes charging stations, AC and DC chargers, electrical systems, software platforms, payment solutions, maintenance, and network management—all working together to deliver a reliable charging experience. In this guide, we’ll explore how EV charging infrastructure is evolving in India, the technologies powering modern charging networks, the role of charging hardware and software, and what this growth means for EV owners and businesses. India’s EV Market at a Glance (June 2026) Metric Latest Data Passenger EV sales (Jun 2026) 31,388 units Passenger EV market penetration 7.7% Passenger EV penetration (Jun 2025) 4.8% Tata Motors market share 38.5% Mahindra market share 24.5% JSW MG market share 18.5% What Is EV Charging Infrastructure? EV charging infrastructure refers to the complete ecosystem that enables electric vehicles to charge safely, efficiently, and reliably. While many people think only of EV charging stations, the infrastructure extends much further. It includes charging hardware, electrical systems, software platforms, payment solutions, monitoring tools, and the operational support required to keep charging networks running smoothly. A typical EV charging infrastructure includes: EV charging stations AC and DC chargers Power supply and electrical distribution Charging connectors and communication protocols Charging management software Payment and user authentication systems Network monitoring and maintenance services Each component plays a different role. Charging hardware delivers electricity to the vehicle, while charging software manages charger availability, charging sessions, payments, diagnostics, and remote monitoring. Together, these components create a connected EV charging network that supports reliable charging for both daily commuting and long-distance travel. EV Charging Hardware Manufacturers in India Reliable EV charging infrastructure starts with reliable charging hardware. As India’s EV charging infrastructure expands, the demand for dependable charging hardware continues to grow. Today, several manufacturers are developing AC chargers, DC fast chargers, portable chargers, and commercial charging solutions to support homes, businesses, highways, and public charging networks. Some of the well-known EV charging hardware manufacturers in India include Exicom, Servotech, Delta Electronics India, Okaya EV, BrightBlu, ABB India, and Statiq , among others. Different charging environments require different types of hardware. AC chargers are commonly installed in homes, apartments, workplaces, and commercial parking spaces, while DC fast chargers are designed for highways, fleet hubs, fuel stations, and other high-traffic locations where faster charging is essential. Among these manufacturers, Statiq offers charging solutions for a wide range of use cases. Its portfolio includes the Nectar Smart Home EV Charger (7.4 kW, 11 kW, and 22 kW), Flow Portable EV Chargers (3.3 kW and 7.4 kW), the AdWall AC Charger for commercial locations, and DC fast chargers ranging from 60 kW to 360 kW . AC vs DC Chargers: Which Charging Infrastructure Does India Need More? A reliable EV charging infrastructure requires both AC chargers and DC fast chargers, as each serves a different charging need. AC chargers are designed for longer parking durations, making them ideal for homes, apartments, workplaces, hotels, and shopping centres. Since most private vehicles remain parked for several hours each day, AC charging is often the most practical and cost-effective solution for everyday charging. DC fast chargers, on the other hand, are built for speed. They convert AC power into DC within the charger itself, allowing electricity to flow directly to the vehicle’s battery. This significantly reduces charging time, making DC fast charging ideal for highways, fuel stations, fleet depots, and other high-traffic commercial locations. Rather than competing with each other, AC and DC chargers complement one another within India’s EV charging infrastructure. While AC chargers support routine daily charging, DC fast chargers enable convenient long-distance travel and faster turnaround times for commercial and fleet operations. To learn more about different charging solutions, explore Statiq’s AC Chargers and DC Fast Chargers designed for homes, businesses, and public charging infrastructure. What Software Powers Modern EV Charging Infrastructure? Installing charging hardware is only one part of building a reliable EV charging network. Behind every connected charging station is software that helps manage charger availability, monitor charging sessions, process payments, detect faults, and keep the network running efficiently. As charging infrastructure expands, software has become essential for operating large charging networks across multiple locations. Modern EV charging infrastructure typically relies on charging management software, interoperability platforms, project management tools, and user-facing mobile apps to support day-to-day network operations. Within its charging ecosystem, Statiq uses an integrated software stack to manage different aspects of EV charging infrastructure. Its Charging Station Management System (CSMS) monitors charger status, charging sessions, payments, user access, and network uptime in real time. For charging interoperability, EVlinq connects multiple charging networks through a single integration, making it easier for charge point operators (CPOs), OEMs, fleet operators, and eMSPs to access shared charging infrastructure. Cristalina manages EV charging infrastructure projects from planning and installation to commissioning and site go-live. For EV users, the Statiq EV Charging App provides a single platform to find nearby charging stations, check real-time availability, reserve chargers, make payments, and manage charging sessions. Together, these software solutions help improve network reliability, operational efficiency, and scalability as India’s EV charging infrastructure continues to expand. How Can Businesses Contribute to India’s EV Charging Infrastructure? The expansion of EV charging infrastructure is creating new opportunities not only for EV drivers but also for businesses. Commercial property owners, hotels, fuel stations, fleet operators, shopping centres, and infrastructure investors are increasingly installing EV charging stations to meet rising demand while creating new revenue opportunities. To support different operational requirements, Statiq offers multiple deployment models. For investors seeking a more hands-off approach, the FOCO (Franchise Owned, Company Operated) model allows them to own EV charging infrastructure while Statiq manages procurement, installation, operations, maintenance, customer support, and billing. Those looking for greater operational control can choose the Direct Ownership Model , which provides full ownership of the charging infrastructure along with flexible pricing and branding options. Statiq also supports commercial fleet operators with dedicated fleet charging infrastructure, enabling the deployment of AC and DC charging hubs backed by intelligent charging management tools. As EV adoption continues to grow, these deployment models are helping expand EV charging infrastructure across highways, commercial properties, workplaces, and fleet operations. Challenges in India’s EV Charging Infrastructure Despite this progress, India’s EV charging infrastructure still faces several challenges as EV adoption continues to grow. One of the biggest challenges is ensuring that charging infrastructure keeps pace with the increasing number of electric vehicles on the road. While major cities and highways continue to see rapid expansion, charger availability can still vary across different regions. Other key challenges include: Expanding charging infrastructure in smaller cities and rural areas Upgrading power infrastructure to support high-capacity DC fast chargers Reducing charger downtime through better monitoring and maintenance Improving interoperability between different charging networks Providing convenient charging access for apartment residents and shared parking spaces Addressing these challenges will require continued collaboration between government agencies, charging network operators, utilities, vehicle manufacturers, and private businesses. Conclusion India’s EV charging infrastructure is evolving rapidly to support the country’s expanding electric vehicle market. As more people switch to EVs, the demand for reliable charging stations, smarter charging software, and accessible AC and DC charging solutions will continue to increase. This growing demand is creating opportunities across the EV charging ecosystem, from EV charging hardware and intelligent software to public charging networks and EV charging station franchise models. Companies like Statiq are contributing to this transition by expanding charging infrastructure through integrated hardware, software, and business solutions, helping make EV charging more accessible across India. Whether you’re an EV owner looking for a reliable EV charging station or a business exploring opportunities in the sector, understanding how EV charging infrastructure is evolving can help you make informed decisions as India’s electric mobility ecosystem continues to expand. FAQs What is EV charging infrastructure? EV charging infrastructure refers to the complete ecosystem that supports electric vehicle charging. It includes EV charging stations, AC and DC chargers, electrical infrastructure, charging software, payment systems, monitoring tools, and maintenance services. Why is EV charging infrastructure important? Reliable EV charging infrastructure makes electric vehicle ownership more practical by improving charging accessibility, reducing range anxiety, and supporting both daily commuting and long-distance travel. What is the difference between an EV charging station and EV charging infrastructure? An EV charging station is a physical location where electric vehicles are charged. EV charging infrastructure is the broader ecosystem that includes charging stations, charging hardware, software platforms, electrical systems, network management, and operational support. How do AC and DC chargers differ? AC chargers deliver alternating current and are commonly used for home, workplace, and destination charging. DC fast chargers convert power within the charger and deliver direct current to the battery, enabling much faster charging at highways, public charging stations, and fleet hubs. 5. What software is used to manage EV charging infrastructure? Modern EV charging infrastructure relies on software to manage chargers, monitor charging sessions, process payments, and maintain network uptime. Within its ecosystem, Statiq uses CSMS, EVlinq, and Cristalina, while the Statiq EV Charging App helps users find chargers, check availability, reserve charging slots, and make payments. 6. How much does it cost to install EV charging infrastructure in India? The cost of installing EV charging infrastructure depends on factors such as charger type, charging capacity, electrical upgrades, civil work, and site requirements. Residential AC chargers require a lower investment, while commercial DC fast charging infrastructure typically involves higher installation costs. 7. Can I install EV charging infrastructure at home? Yes. Home EV charging infrastructure typically includes an AC charger or wall-mounted charger installed with proper electrical wiring and safety measures. It offers a convenient and cost-effective way to charge an electric vehicle overnight. title: Granite Awarded $50 Million Contract for Tiger Creek Regulator Dam Spillway Replacement
summary: WATSONVILLE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Granite (NYSE:GVA) announced today that it has been awarded an approximately $50 million contract by Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) for the Tiger Creek Regulator Dam Spillway Replacement proj
body_text: WATSONVILLE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Granite (NYSE:GVA) announced today that it has been awarded an approximately $50 million contract by Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) for the Tiger Creek Regulator Dam Spillway Replacement project in Amador County, California, near Pioneer. The project will be included in Granite’s second quarter 2026 CAP. The project, part of PG&E’s Mokelumne River Hydroelectric Project, involves construction of a new spillway that will replace an existing structure at the Tiger Creek Regulator Dam, a slab and buttress dam originally constructed in 1931. The project will enhance long-term dam safety, improve operational reliability, and ensure compliance with updated regulatory and engineering standards. Granite’s scope of work includes construction of the new spillway crest structure and chute, installation of a temporary cofferdam to allow work to be performed in dry conditions, excavation and rock anchoring, placement of mass and structural concrete, and decommissioning of the existing spillway. The project also includes improvements to site access, including construction of a permanent access road to support ongoing maintenance of the new spillway. A separate preconstruction contract, completed in 2024 with an approximate value of $600,000, supported early planning and constructability efforts for the project. “We have a long history of building critical dam projects for many clients in Northern California including the Folsom Dam Auxiliary Spillway Control Structure, Mormon Island Auxiliary Dam, Lost Creek Dam, and Log Pond Dam,” says Bob Mihal, Granite Area Manager. “Our team brings deep technical expertise and a collaborative approach, and we look forward to serving PG&E and strengthening our partnership on critical infrastructure that supports the region’s communities.” Construction began in May 2026, with completion anticipated in May 2028. About Granite Granite is America’s Infrastructure Company™. Incorporated since 1922, Granite (NYSE:GVA) is one of the largest diversified construction and construction materials companies in the United States as well as a full-suite civil construction provider. Granite’s Code of Conduct and strong Core Values guide the Company and its employees to uphold the highest ethical standards. Granite is an industry leader in safety and an award-winning firm in quality and sustainability. For more information, visit the Granite website, graniteconstruction.com , and connect with Granite on LinkedIn , X , Facebook ,and Instagram .
